issue_context.title: [umbrella issue]: poor visibility/observability of the kubelet (cpu,memory,device,topology) managers
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

The kubelet {cpu, memory, device, topology} manager, collectively known as resource managers, give little to none feedback to their consumers. Once the kubelet is configured with the relevant settings (e.g. cpuManagerPolicy=static or topologyManagerPolicy=restricted, say) and once the workload requests exclusive resources provided by the managers, the implicit contract is that if the pod is admitted, then all the resources are provisioned according to the spec. Similarly, if the kubelet cannot allocate the resources as requested (and as configured) the pod will fail admission with a TopologyAffinityError or similar generic error.

The problem is twofold:
- there's no **explicit** feedback about resource allocation. For example, the system explicitly acknowledges a pod got its image pulled succesfully with a event, yet it does not for resource allocation, even though both are arguably prerequisites to have the pod running, and both could be theoretically inferred from the fact the pod started. The point of this example is to highlight the lack of explicit feedback about allocation.
- on error, there's no way to learn what gone wrong except in most generic term (pod failed with TopologyAffinityError). The only option is to look at kubelet logs, but the kubelet verbosity has to be >= 4 anyway.

### What did you expect to happen?

On success, the system should somehow explcitely acknowledge the resource classes being allocated, for example "CPUs" and that NUMA alignment took place.

On admission failure, the system should give indication of what caused admission failure, like unable to allocate enough memory on the selected NUMA zone, or missing device affine to the selected NUMA zone. But any more information that is presented now is welcome.

In both cases we probably don't want or need to expose the details of the concrete resources, at least not initially.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. succesfully run a pod requiring a device, or exclusive access to CPUs, or NUMA alignment. Observe lack of feedback.
2. try to run a pod requiring a device or exclusive access to CPUs, or NUMA alignment. Make it fail admission (e.g. ask for more CPUs than existing on the machine's NUMA zone). Observe the error is a generic "TopologyAffinityError" with lack of indication about the resource failed to be allocated

### Anything else we need to know?

The observability, or lack thereof, of the resource management subsystem was also a [recurring theme in the related Production Readiness Reviews](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/CPNHUMN74/p1696357853594279), culminating in a [blocking comment](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/CPNHUMN74/p1696518756979339?thread_ts=1696357853.594279&cid=CPNHUMN74) for memory manager GA graduation.

### Kubernetes version

<details>
any since 1.18 (cpumanager introduced, the first of resource managers)
</details>

Regarding log improvements, I believe the best way forward is to improve the resource managers (cpumanager, devicemanager, memorymanager, topologymanager) to make use of contextual logging (see: 
https://kubernetes.io/blog/2020/09/04/kubernetes-1-19-introducing-structured-logs/
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/1602-structured-logging/README.md
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+contextual+logging)
using contextual logging solves most of the problems in logs, maing easier to follow the code flow and having a common experience across the project.
As followup work we can review the logs to check if something else can be improved, like reviewing the verbosiness, adding key=value pairs, improving the messages or anything else, but should be a followup after the move to contextual logging.

review_comments:
the nuance we lose here is the different log level in the logs, these will be now presented as ERRs which may be caught differently from alerts/monitoring tools. OTOH all this recoverable errors ARE worth an alert at least (we saw similar things in other resource managers).

Arguably, we should actually take the error path and do not swallow these errors, but this will change a long established behavior, so the fix can be worse than the issue.

TL;DR: I'm happier with this change than with the existing code.

I agree that changing the log level to `ERR` might impact monitoring systems differently, but given that these recoverable errors are still significant, I think they warrant better visibility. Other resource managers already follow a similar pattern, so this aligns with existing behavior elsewhere.

That said, I understand the concern about modifying long-standing behavior. I think we should capture this in the resource management logging guideline that I would like to publish soon. 

Let me know if you think there's a better way to handle this or if adding to the guideline addresses your concerns.

Clarification: the current change I think is beneficial for the reasons above. We may need a targeted revert of this very commit in the worst case, which is bearable.

The change of long-established behavior would be a followup hypotethical change on which we actually err out in the error paths on which currently we log ERR and continue. THAT would change a long established (debatable) behavior and THAT fix could likely be worse than the small "issue" this current change here is provoking.

So I think we should go along with this change with no further action until (if ever) further evidence comes out
the same here. Are there any guidelines regarding this?

For the same reasons as mentioned earlier: minimizing noise and maintaining consistency across resource managers. Please refer to the previous CPU Manager logging improvement for context: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120569/commits/2dc5ddd08a41a171134fd0922825ed03faa379ca.

Unfortunately, I haven't found guidelines/recommendations with this level of details in Kubernetes documentation. I know @pohly is quiet active in this area and might know?

I have been drafting some guidelines as I am working through the resource managers and am happy to contribute this for future reference but I am not sure where? :)
I've seen some guidelines made by @pohly in the DRA code, but I don't remember where exactly. @pohly can you help?

Guidelines for logging levels? https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/logging.md#what-method-to-use might be what you look for.

It's up to the code owners to decide which things are useful enough to be logged more often.
